tip: 'paid â' tells one person not to do something: 'paid â rhoi'r gorau' means don't give up.
'buon ni' means we were, the plain past of 'bod' (to be); the '-on ni' ending is the we part.
The ending '-odd' marks a past he or she: 'canu' becomes 'canodd hi' (she sang).
Before an m sound, 'yn' (in) becomes 'ym': 'pobman' turns into 'ym mhobman', 'p' mutating to 'mh'.
Welsh has no verb for have: 'mae gen i brofiad' is literally there is with me experience, meaning I have experience.
After 'pum' (five), 'blynedd' becomes 'mlynedd': 'pum mlynedd'. Some numbers nasal-mutate the following noun.
An adjective softens after a feminine noun: 'miniog' becomes 'finiog' in 'cyllell finiog' (sharp knife).
'ers' marks time still ongoing: 'ers deng mlynedd' means for ten years and counting, up to now.
The ending '-af' makes the most: 'hir' (long) becomes 'hiraf' (longest) in 'yr afon hiraf'.
'dyma' means here is or this is, pointing at what is in front of you: 'dyma'r traeth', this is the beach.
Feelings sit on you: 'mae hiraeth dwfn arna i' means I feel a deep longing, where 'arna i' is 'ar' (on) plus me.
'chwe' (six) triggers aspirate mutation, so 'cant' becomes 'chant', as in 'chwe chant' (six hundred).
'sawl' (how many) always takes a singular noun, so it is 'sawl plentyn' (how many children), never a plural.
'gyda' triggers aspirate mutation, so 'pob' becomes 'phob' in 'gyda phob parch' (with all respect).
'ymdrech' is feminine, so a following adjective soft-mutates: 'bach' becomes 'fach' in 'ymdrech fach' (small effort).
'ar' triggers soft mutation, so 'dydd' becomes 'ddydd': 'ar ddydd Sadwrn' (on Saturday).
'bydd' is the future of 'bod' (to be): 'bydd y tywydd yn heulog' means the weather will be sunny.
'paid â' plus a verb is the singular way to say don't; 'â' becomes 'ag' before a vowel: 'paid ag anghofio' (don't forget).
The linking 'yn' softens a following adjective, so 'cynnar' becomes 'gynnar': 'di'n gynnar' (you finish early).
'hyd y gwn i' is a set phrase for as far as I know; 'gwn' is I know, from 'gwybod'.
'dadl' is feminine, so it soft-mutates after the article: 'mae'r ddadl' (the debate).
Possession uses 'mae gan', and the thing owned soft-mutates: 'ci' becomes 'gi' in 'mae gan Eluned gi' (Eluned has a dog).
After a one-word verb like 'prynodd' (bought), the object soft-mutates: 'papur' becomes 'bapur' in 'prynodd Rhodri bapur'.
'ei' (her) triggers aspirate mutation, so 'pen-blwydd' becomes 'phen-blwydd': 'ei phen-blwydd' (her birthday).
'cystal' is the as-good-as form of 'da' (good), meaning as good as: 'cystal ag unrhyw gaws' (as good as any cheese).
'roedd' plus 'wedi' makes the had-done past: 'roedd hi wedi ymarfer' means she had practised.
'fel na' plus 'fyddai' means so that ... would not: 'fel na fyddai'r defaid yn dianc' (so the sheep would not escape).
'erbyn' marks a deadline, meaning by a point in time: 'erbyn 2050' (by 2050).
The '-wch' ending makes a command plural or polite: 'sefwch' means stand to a group or formally.
Welsh has no verb have: 'mae gen i' means I have, literally there is with me: 'mae gen i anifail anwes'.
